routes.description: Establish a personal transcendent creator through the universe's beginning, connect objective morality to a good divine foundation, and use the resurrection case to identify the creator with Christian theism, while showing that observed suffering and the evil-God analogy do not defeat that cumulative case.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its origin, moral, and resurrection components jointly support the Christian God and if the evidential inference from suffering is undercut by morally sufficient reasons or limits on human probability judgments without leaving the evil-God hypothesis evidentially symmetrical.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative arguments must support the existence of the Christian God strongly enough to withstand both the evidential problem of suffering and the evil-God symmetry challenge.

centralBridges.description: The universe's beginning must warrant a transcendent, immaterial, timeless, powerful, personal cause rather than mere unexplained origin.
Objective moral values and duties must require a divine foundation capable of supplying the creator's good moral character.
The historical resurrection case must discriminate in favor of divine action and connect generic creator reasoning to specifically Christian theism.
Apparently gratuitous suffering and the mirrored evil-God hypothesis must not warrant rejection of a good God once the full cumulative case and possible divine purposes are considered.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Human cognitive and historical limitations must materially constrain judgments that particular suffering lacks a morally sufficient providential purpose.
Divine goodness must rest on grounds other than a simple inductive inventory of worldly goods if the observational mirror is to misdescribe the theistic inference.

routes.description: Use the scale of apparently gratuitous suffering to disconfirm an omnipotent good God, show that standard defenses and appeals to inscrutable purposes transfer to an evil creator, and contest whether the cosmological, moral, and resurrection arguments supply the asymmetry or cumulative support required for Christian theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if suffering remains substantial evidence against the good-God hypothesis, Craig's defenses fail to distinguish it from the parallel evil-God hypothesis, and the affirmative arguments do not independently establish the creator's goodness or specifically Christian identity strongly enough to overcome that challenge.

motionBridge.description: Observed suffering and evil-God symmetry must prevent Craig's cumulative arguments from establishing the good Christian God specified by the motion.

centralBridges.description: The quantity, intensity, and history of sentient suffering must provide evidential grounds for excluding an omnipotent and perfectly good deity.
Free will, stable laws, soul-making, compensation, and unknown-purpose defenses must be shown to transfer materially from a good God to an evil creator.
The moral argument must fail to establish a divine foundation for objective morality capable of breaking the good-God and evil-God symmetry.
The cosmological and resurrection arguments must fail to identify a good Christian God or to outweigh the observational evidence invoked against that hypothesis.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Rational exclusion of a specified deity must remain possible even without a complete alternative explanation of cosmic origins or suffering.
The evidential challenge must be formulable through excessive suffering without presupposing objective evil or the moral realism disputed by the moral argument.

sections.title: Cosmological Cause and the Creator's Moral Character
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the universe's beginning establishes a personal transcendent creator and whether that conclusion contributes anything toward choosing between a good creator, an evil creator, and a morally unspecified cause.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Its Proposed Divine Foundation
sections.rationale: The moral argument is the principal bridge from a morally neutral creator to divine goodness, while its premises, atheist-compatible alternatives, and relationship to suffering determine whether it can break the central symmetry.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Christian Identification
sections.rationale: The resurrection argument supplies the specifically Christian component of the cumulative case, making the reliability and discriminatory force of extraordinary historical testimony necessary issues rather than merely generic evidence for a creator.

sections.title: Suffering, Feasible Worlds, and Morally Sufficient Reasons
sections.rationale: The scale of sentient suffering is the principal observational evidence against a perfectly good God, and the dispute over feasible alternatives, providential purposes, and human epistemic limits directly governs that inference.

sections.title: Evil-God Symmetry and Observational Inference
sections.rationale: The defining comparative challenge asks whether defenses of a good God can be mirrored for an evil creator and whether observation may exclude a morally specified deity without serving as a positive argument for its opposite.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Because the universe began to exist, it has an uncaused, timeless, immaterial, and personal transcendent cause.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig at the podium, and the uninterrupted opening address remains his until the next speaker transition.

response.rationale: This is a constructive opening argument, so it has no earlier opposing target; it directly supplies the proposed transcendent-cause bridge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly presents the core deduction and several claimed attributes.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogism is recoverable, but the move compresses the further transition from a transcendent cause to a personal cause.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Necessity fits the stated syllogism conditionally, but not every attributed property follows with equal explicitness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The basic conclusion follows if both premises hold, but the personal-cause bridge remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt states the premises and attributes but does not provide representative support or compare origin alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the indispensable central bridge to a transcendent personal cause.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing alternative is assessed in this constructive span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly states that the universe began, that whatever begins has a transcendent cause, and then attributes timelessness and immateriality to that cause.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist and require God as their transcendent foundation, thereby supporting God's existence and goodness.
moves.attributionBasis: This numbered argument occurs within Craig's uninterrupted opening address after his cosmological case and before his historical case.

response.rationale: This constructive move has no reply target and directly advances the proposed bridge from objective morality to divine existence and goodness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, the principal conditional and intended moral-character function are explicit.

precisionFindings.rationale: Objective values are defined, though the requirement that only God can ground them is left as an implicit defended qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical divine-ground requirement exceeds the support visible in the selected evidence and lacks an alternative-ground caveat.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional structure is usable, but the exclusive bridge from objectivity to God is a material unsupported premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move defines objective morality but substantially asserts rather than defends its uniquely divine foundation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central bridge intended to establish the creator's good moral character.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive excerpt does not engage a developed competing account of objective morality.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig expressly says the first argument does not establish moral character and introduces the premise that objective values and duties would not exist without God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples' resulting belief are best explained by Jesus's resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces his third numbered argument and develops it continuously until beginning the summary of his opening case.

response.rationale: This constructive move has no prior opposing target and supplies the historical component intended to identify the creator with Christian theism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states three facts and the proposed best explanation compactly and directly.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three claims and explanatory conclusion are clear, though the evidential and comparative qualifications remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling resurrection the best explanation requires source reliability and serious rival comparison not present in this span.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive structure is coherent, but the bridge from the three reports to resurrection is materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt enumerates historical claims without documenting their independence, reliability, or superiority to rival explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central resurrection-identification bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: No natural alternative is developed or assessed in this constructive excerpt.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source identifies the empty tomb, appearances, and disciples' belief as historical facts and asserts that resurrection best explains them.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: The immense scale and depth of apparently gratuitous animal and human suffering provide powerful evidence against an omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Law, who announces one opening argument and develops the evidential problem of evil throughout this uninterrupted passage.

response.rationale: This is a constructive evidential argument with no earlier opposing target; it supplies the observational suffering premise central to the negative route.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states the evidential datum, divine-reason requirement, and disconfirming consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is explicitly probabilistic and specifies the relevant deity and aggregate scale of suffering.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The probabilistic force is appropriate, though the selected span gives limited support for judging all suffering inexplicable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The likelihood-based inference is coherent, with only the comparative expectation under perfect goodness compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The vast historical scale is a relevant datum, but representativeness and alternative-purpose comparison are underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central observational-suffering bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents its positive evidential case before developed theistic replies are available.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law cites suffering across eons and argues that perfect goodness requires an adequate reason for every instance, making the apparent excess powerful contrary evidence.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: Good-God belief faces a symmetry challenge because observed suffering counts against it just as observed goodness counts against an otherwise parallel evil-God hypothesis.
moves.attributionBasis: Law remains the sole speaker and explicitly pivots from his evidential argument to an alternative evil-creator hypothesis and its mirrored problem.

components.text: Whether the cosmological cause supplies grounds for a morally good rather than morally unspecified creator.
Whether Craig's separate moral argument can provide the missing asymmetry in the creator's character.

response.rationale: The reply directly contacts the cosmological move's failure to establish moral character, but this span does not yet answer the distinct divine-ground premise of the moral argument.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer contacting the decisive limitation of the cosmological conclusion while leaving the moral bridge unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Despite a verbal restart, the proposition and its restriction to moral character are recoverable and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move limits its conclusion to the absence of moral-character support from the cosmological argument.

charity.alternative: The cosmological argument is intended only to establish a personal creator, with goodness supplied cumulatively by another argument.
charity.decisiveQualification: That limitation concedes the cosmological component alone does not distinguish good from evil creator hypotheses.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The component-level symmetry follows cleanly from the stated moral neutrality of the cosmological cause.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant rests directly on the limited content of Craig's stated cosmological conclusion, with only broader cumulative comparison deferred.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the negative motion route by identifying a major symmetry in the cumulative case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the cumulative structure while accurately isolating the cosmological component's moral neutrality.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law explicitly says Craig's cosmological argument gives no clue about the creator's moral character and therefore supports good- and evil-creator hypotheses equally at that stage.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: Free will, stable natural laws, soul-making, inscrutable purposes, and afterlife compensation can be mirrored to explain goodness under an evil God, so those defenses do not distinguish the good-God hypothesis.
moves.attributionBasis: Law continuously develops mirrored versions of familiar theodicies within his opening turn, with no intervening change of speaker or topic ownership.

response.rationale: This constructive symmetry move has no reply target and supplies the central claim that standard good-God defenses can be reversed for an evil creator.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it develops multiple concrete mirrored defenses rather than merely asserting symmetry.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly claims material transfer of specified defense types, not strict identity in every detail.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The illustrative force matches the supplied mirrored examples and does not require certainty that every possible defense transfers.

charity.alternative: Free will, natural law, soul-making, compensation, and unknown purposes may jointly explain suffering under a good God.
charity.decisiveQualification: Structurally parallel considerations can be formulated to explain goods under an evil creator unless an independent moral asymmetry is supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogical inference is consistent and supported by several explicit mappings, though exact parity is not fully demonstrated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several representative mirrored defenses support the claim, with a bounded gap concerning their full comparative plausibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central mirrored-defenses bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move engages recognizable strong versions of several theodicies and identifies the precise comparative limitation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly flips a standard free-will theodicy and begins a parallel treatment of law-governed nature, within a span covering further mirrored defenses.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: If abundant goodness makes an evil God highly unlikely despite mirrored defenses, abundant suffering should likewise make a good God highly unlikely unless a relevant asymmetry is established.
moves.attributionBasis: Law concludes his opening case in a continuous passage explicitly framing the challenge he is placing before Craig for the ensuing response.

components.text: Whether an independent moral asymmetry justifies treating abundant suffering differently from abundant goodness.
Whether a morally neutral creator conclusion can itself break the good-creator and evil-creator symmetry.
Whether specifically Christian historical evidence independently outweighs the observational parity challenge.

response.rationale: The parity argument contacts the need for a relevant moral asymmetry and the cosmological argument's neutrality, but it does not assess the resurrection evidence in this span.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a strong partial answer because it states the decisive symmetry demand while leaving one cumulative component untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly conditional on the absence of a relevant asymmetry and remains probabilistic.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted likelihood conclusion is appropriately conditional and mirrors the admitted observational exclusion of an evil creator.

charity.alternative: Possible morally sufficient reasons can make suffering compatible with a good God.
charity.decisiveQualification: Comparable possible reasons can preserve an evil creator despite goodness, yet observation is still treated as rationally excluding that hypothesis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity inference is explicit and consistent, with the need for an independent asymmetry clearly identified.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The comparison is well illustrated, though full likelihood assignments for the two hypotheses are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly states the defining negative route-completion challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move grants the defensive possibilities and targets their inability by themselves to defeat comparative observational evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law grants ingenious evil-God defenses yet says abundant goodness still rationally excludes that deity, then asks why abundant suffering should not analogously exclude a good God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Observed suffering does not defeat God unless it is probable that God lacks morally sufficient reasons and that a better feasible world was available.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig's first response, and Craig directly identifies Law's evidential problem before presenting this uninterrupted initial rebuttal.

components.text: Whether apparently gratuitous suffering makes it probable that God has no morally sufficient reasons.
Whether merely possible unknown purposes establish a relevant asymmetry from the evil-creator case.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the probability premise of the suffering inference and invokes feasible-world constraints, but it does not distinguish the mirrored evil-creator defense.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the decisive evidential premise while leaving the symmetry component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The probability demand is clear, but the shift between what must be proved and what must merely be probable creates a material scope tension.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Possible providential reasons undercut certainty but do not alone defeat the comparative probability claimed by the evidential argument.

charity.alternative: The amount and pattern of suffering can lower the probability of perfect goodness without proving that no sufficient reason is possible.
charity.decisiveQualification: An evidential argument needs comparative improbability, not proof of impossibility or access to a better feasible world.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The possibility of sufficient reasons is coherent, but treating it as defeating a probabilistic inference leaves a substantial modal gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The suggested salvation-maximizing world is speculative and no comparative support establishes its probability or feasibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central observational-suffering bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply materially raises the opponent's burden from probabilistic evidence to proof while only briefly acknowledging improbability.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig says the atheist must show that sufficient reasons are impossible or highly improbable and speculates that suffering may be necessary for maximizing freely obtained salvation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Evil-God symmetry does not undermine theism because divine goodness is not inferred from an inventory of worldly goods, and an evil creator would not be worship-worthy God.
moves.attributionBasis: This is a continuous portion of Craig's explicitly introduced rebuttal, with first-person references to his own argument.

components.text: Whether observational parity applies when divine goodness is not inferred inductively from worldly goods.
Whether the concrete mirrored theodicies remain equally effective for an evil creator.
Whether changing the label from evil God to evil creator resolves the evidential symmetry.

response.rationale: The response contacts Law's inductive framing and corrects the worship-worthiness terminology, but does not answer the material transfer of the mirrored defenses.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive framing component but leaves the strongest concrete symmetry evidence substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The God versus creator distinction is explicit, but redefining God as worship-worthy risks making the terminological point substitute for the substantive hypothesis.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The response correctly limits the source of Craig's goodness inference, but does not establish that this removes the observational comparison.

charity.alternative: The evil-God challenge concerns an omnipotent evil creator, regardless of whether that being is called God or worship-worthy.
charity.decisiveQualification: Renaming the hypothesis does not remove its intended evidential comparison with a perfectly good creator.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The noninductive-ground point is relevant, but worship-worthiness does not logically defeat the parallel evil-creator hypothesis.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move asserts a noninductive foundation without supplying the promised argument that observation cannot bear symmetrically.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central mirrored-defenses bridge, though incompletely.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes the evil-creator hypothesis but gives undue argumentative weight to the terminological distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig distinguishes an evil creator from a worship-worthy God and says divine goodness is not inferred from a simple inventory of worldly goods.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: The evidential challenge can be framed solely in terms of apparently excessive suffering, so it neither presupposes objective evil nor depends upon moral realism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Law's rebuttal, and Law explicitly identifies and answers Craig's claim that evil proves God.

components.text: Whether the suffering objection depends on the atheist affirming objective evil or moral realism.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses that the evidential argument needs only excessive suffering, not an atheist commitment to objective evil, and states that moral nihilism is compatible with the challenge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies and defeats the targeted presupposition while preserving the evidential issue.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between suffering and objective evil is explicit and consistently scoped to the evidential argument.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The structural claim about what the argument requires is directly demonstrated by its reformulation.

charity.alternative: An atheist's appeal to evil may appear to presuppose objective moral values that atheism cannot ground.
charity.decisiveQualification: The same likelihood challenge can be stated using suffering and the good God's own stipulated aims without atheist moral realism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reformulation directly removes the alleged premise without changing the evidential structure.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual demonstration is sufficient for the limited structural claim, with no substantial empirical gap.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It fully supplies the subsidiary bridge allowing suffering evidence without moral realism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the strongest internal-consistency concern and supplies a narrower formulation that avoids it.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law explicitly says a moral nihilist can run the argument from the enormous and apparently excessive amount of suffering without invoking good or evil.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: Craig has not established that objective moral values exist or that they require God, and combining those premises with the evidence of suffering may support moral skepticism rather than theism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Law's next rebuttal, and Law explicitly turns to Craig's arguments before sustaining a detailed critique of the moral argument.

components.text: Whether objective moral values exist and, if so, whether their existence requires God.
Whether suffering instead supplies counterevidence against the proposed moral foundation.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests both premises of the moral argument and connects suffering to a rival skeptical inference, though some support relies on authority and compressed alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive premises and supplies contrary implications rather than merely changing topics.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenges to existence, divine necessity, and the alternative skeptical implication are separately recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that Craig has not established the premises fits, but philosopher disagreement alone has limited evidential force.

charity.alternative: Objective moral values may be grounded in God's nature and duties in divine commands.
charity.decisiveQualification: That account still requires reasons to reject atheist-compatible realism and to reconcile its good foundation with suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The premise attacks and counterevidential inference are coherent, though the move compresses the route from suffering to moral skepticism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It identifies relevant disagreement and counterevidence but relies substantially on authority and does not develop atheist grounding alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central no-moral-asymmetry bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response engages the principal divine-ground claim fairly, with a bounded omission concerning its strongest metaphysical development.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law restates the moral syllogism, cites philosophical rejection including Swinburne, disputes both premises, and argues suffering can push the combined evidence toward skepticism.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: Baffling and apparently corroborated testimony is expected to arise occasionally even without miracles, so the resurrection reports provide little support unless they discriminate against that baseline expectation.
moves.attributionBasis: Law explicitly turns to the resurrection argument and carries the resulting analogy and evidential conclusion through the delivered lookahead.

components.text: Whether apparently baffling testimony discriminates resurrection from the baseline occurrence of hard-to-explain reports.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the missing likelihood comparison in the resurrection inference and states why baffling testimony alone offers little support when such cases are independently expected.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the decisive abductive inference and states the defeating base-rate consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The likelihood requirement and baseline class of baffling reports are clearly identified and appropriately qualified as occasional.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited conclusion of little support absent discrimination matches the stated base-rate argument.

charity.alternative: The resurrection reports may be unusually early, multiple, and corroborated rather than merely baffling.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those features support resurrection only if shown substantially less expected under mundane report-generating processes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The Bayesian discrimination requirement is explicit and directly bears on the best-explanation inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The baseline point is well motivated conceptually, but the actual frequency and similarity of comparison cases are not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central resurrection-identification bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response allows unusually difficult cases but correctly insists on the comparative likelihood question.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law states that evidence supports a hypothesis when expected on it and unexpected otherwise, then argues that baffling reports occur occasionally even without miracles.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Atheism supplies no adequate account of objective moral values and duties, whereas God's nature and commands provide a transcendent foundation for them.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig continues his announced summation, addresses Law by name, and restates the premises and explanatory rationale of his moral argument.

components.text: Whether atheism offers an adequate grounding account for objective moral values and duties.
Whether the suffering argument can proceed without objective morality.

response.rationale: The reply contacts Law's failure to provide an atheist moral ontology and offers God's nature and commands, but it does not answer the moral-realism-independent suffering formulation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a partial answer that addresses the grounding demand while leaving the separate suffering reformulation untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative explanation is clear, though what counts as adequate grounding and how nature and commands divide roles remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Offering an account gives comparative relevance, but absence of an account in Law's span does not itself establish theism's adequacy.

charity.alternative: An atheist can deny objective morality or accept a nondivine realist account without presenting a full theory in this debate.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig may still press that Law has not supplied such an account, but that omission does not eliminate those live positions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative inference is intelligible, but it moves too quickly from no offered atheist account to a better theistic foundation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: God's nature and commands are named as grounds but their explanatory adequacy and rival comparison are substantially asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the negative route's central no-moral-asymmetry bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly notes the missing account but understates the distinction between debate omission and absence of alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig stresses that moral theory should explain the moral realm, says Law offered no account, and proposes God's nature and commands as a transcendent foundation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Jesus's resurrection satisfies explanatory criteria better than natural alternatives and is rendered plausible by the religious-historical context of his life and claims.
moves.attributionBasis: The same uninterrupted Craig summation explicitly turns to the resurrection and contrasts his explanation with Law's paranormal-report analogy.

components.text: Whether the resurrection case has discriminatory explanatory features beyond being merely baffling testimony.

response.rationale: The reply directly invokes comparative explanatory criteria and religious-historical context, but it asserts rather than demonstrates that no natural explanation performs as well.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive discrimination demand, with a bounded comparative-development gap.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criteria and contextual plausibility claim are clear, and the speaker appropriately frames the conclusion as his comparative judgment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The probabilistic framing is apt, but the claimed superiority lacks an exhibited natural-alternative comparison in the selected span.

charity.alternative: Baffling testimony should be expected occasionally from mundane causes and therefore has a weak likelihood ratio.
charity.decisiveQualification: Case-specific explanatory scope, power, and historical context could discriminate only if their comparative performance is actually established.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The criteria-based answer is coherent, though the conclusion depends on an implicit application of those criteria to alternatives.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Relevant criteria and context are supplied, but natural rivals and the historical facts are not specifically compared here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central claim that the resurrection component is insufficient.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response accurately addresses the strongest base-rate challenge while leaving a bounded evidential demonstration gap.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig cites explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and ad hocness, says no natural account performs as well, and invokes Jesus's religious-historical context.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: Even if a cosmological argument established a creator, it would supply no grounds for preferring an all-good creator over an all-evil creator and would not establish Craig's God.
moves.attributionBasis: A moderator question cues Law, who explicitly denies Craig's characterization of his position and explains the restricted scope of his debate strategy.

components.text: Whether a transcendent creator conclusion establishes the perfect goodness required by Craig's God.
Whether the separate moral argument can provide the missing grounds for goodness.
Whether God's nature and commands independently resolve cosmological moral neutrality.

response.rationale: The reply precisely contacts the limitation of the cosmological conclusion while expressly declining to concede that conclusion, but does not answer Craig's separate moral route.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a strong partial answer to the cosmological component, not a full answer to the cumulative moral case.

precisionFindings.rationale: Law explicitly distinguishes a conditional concession for discussion from accepting the cosmological conclusion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that the cosmological argument supplies no moral predicate follows from the content attributed to that argument.

charity.alternative: Craig presents the cosmological argument only as one component, with goodness supplied by the moral argument.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even in a cumulative case, this component itself remains morally neutral and cannot contribute the required asymmetry.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional component analysis is explicit, consistent, and does not confuse restriction with concession.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion is grounded in the stated content of Craig's cosmological move, with only the broader cumulative question deferred.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central transcendent-personal-cause bridge insofar as that bridge is used to reach Craig's morally specified God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply expressly respects the limited component while accurately identifying what it does not establish.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law clarifies that he did not concede a creator and argues conditionally that Craig's first argument gives no reason to prefer an all-good to an all-evil creator.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The cosmological case is a deductive argument requiring denial of either the universe's beginning or its transcendent cause, rather than an appeal to gaps in scientific knowledge.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks whether Law's profession of ignorance is sufficient, and Craig answers in the first person while restating his deductive premises.

components.text: Whether the cosmological conclusion supplies any basis for the creator's perfect goodness.

response.rationale: The reply explains why the argument is deductive rather than gap-based, but Law's selected objection concerned moral neutrality, not whether the argument was a God-of-the-gaps inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is relevant contrary material about the cosmological argument but does not contact the decisive moral-character demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dilemma between denying a premise and accepting the conclusion is clear, as is the distinction from scientific gap reasoning.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional deductive claim is properly limited to accepting the two premises.

logicalCoherence.rationale: As a characterization of the stated syllogism, the deductive structure and premise-denial options are explicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The formal characterization is supported by the argument's form, though the truth of the premises is not defended here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the central transcendent-cause bridge, but does not address the selected moral-neutrality objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span does not engage Law's actual moral-neutrality alternative closely enough for a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig states that an objector must deny either the beginning premise or causal conditional and distinguishes this philosophical deduction from filling scientific gaps.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Human cognitive limitations prevent reliable probability judgments that apparently gratuitous goods or evils lack sufficient purposes in an omniscient being's providential plan.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker refers back to a point previously made from Stephen Wykstra and develops Craig's characteristic skeptical-theist response concerning divine purposes.

components.text: Whether humans can reliably assign probabilities that observed goods or evils are gratuitous under omniscient providence.
Whether apparently excessive suffering supports a reliable likelihood judgment against a good God.
Whether the same skeptical limit equally protects an evil creator from abundant goodness.

response.rationale: The reply directly attacks human access to gratuitousness probabilities for both goods and evils, but it does not establish an asymmetry preventing the same limit from shielding an evil creator.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive probability inference but remains partial because the mirrored consequence is left unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The epistemic limitation is clearly stated for both gratuitous goods and gratuitous evils under an omniscient being.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Cognitive limitation warrants caution, but the claim that no probability judgment is possible is stronger than the support provided.

charity.alternative: Even limited observers may draw defeasible likelihood inferences from the scale and pattern of suffering or goodness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Lack of certainty about total providential consequences does not by itself eliminate all comparative probabilistic evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The limitation premise is relevant, but the categorical inference from limited access to no usable probability is under-supported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Omniscient purposes are invoked abstractly without showing why ordinary defeasible induction becomes wholly unreliable.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that an omniscient controller may have inaccessible ends and therefore humans cannot judge either apparent good or evil gratuitous by induction.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The long-range consequences of historical events exceed human epistemic reach, so observers cannot know that God lacks sufficient reasons for permitting particular suffering.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer recalls Craig's earlier citation of James Clerk Maxwell and articulates a providential ripple-effect account of morally sufficient reasons for suffering.

components.text: Whether observers can know that particular suffering lacks a morally sufficient long-range providential purpose.
Whether long-range ignorance creates a relevant asymmetry rather than equally protecting an evil creator.

response.rationale: The reply supplies a concrete mechanism for epistemic limitation through historical ripple effects, but does not address the parallel evil-creator application.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the suffering inference's decisive epistemic premise but remains partial on the comparative symmetry demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is limited to inability to know the eventual sufficient reason for particular historical events.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Untraceable long-range effects justify uncertainty but do not establish that there is simply no evidentially useful judgment.

charity.alternative: Aggregate suffering may be evidential even if the complete consequences of each event are unknowable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Local ignorance of ripple effects does not automatically defeat a global comparative likelihood inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical mechanism is plausible but asserted without representative cases or comparison to ordinary probabilistic reasoning.
